headline: Bank of Canada Holds at 2.25% for a Fourth Time as Q4 GDP Contracts 0.6% and Oil Hits $100 on the Strait of Hormuz Disruption
executive_summary:
The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25%26 on April 29, 2026, a fourth consecutive hold and unchanged since October 2025. Governing Council said it would look through the war's immediate inflation impact but "will not let higher energy prices become persistent inflation," projecting a return to the 2% target in 2027.28 The prime rate stands at 6.09%. The database tracks 211 residential projects ($32.2B) and 1,663 infrastructure projects ($210.3B) carrying rate-sensitive financing; the next scheduled decision is June 10, 2026.26

Real GDP contracted -0.6% annualized in the fourth quarter of 2025 against a consensus expectation of flat output, and full-year 2025 growth was 1.7%, the slowest pace since 2016 excluding the pandemic, according to Statistics Canada.112 Lower exports, particularly to the U.S. under steel, aluminum and motor-vehicle tariffs, were the main drag. Manufacturing GDP fell 3.1% year-over-year; the database tracks 73 manufacturing projects ($68.8B), and StatCan reported three in ten manufacturers cited a major negative tariff impact with one in five planning to delay investment.112

WTI crude settled near US$100.16/bbl (+5.0% on the week, +60.1% year-over-year) and Brent at US$108.59 (+7.2% on the week) as the Strait of Hormuz disruption cut roughly 4 million barrels per day of flows in March and April; the IEA described the disruption as exceeding the 1970s oil crises in scale.82 The energy move fed inflation: headline CPI rose 2.4% year-over-year in March, up from 1.8% in February, lifted by a record 21.2% month-over-month gasoline increase, and remained within the Bank of Canada's 1-3% target band.106 The database tracks 59 oil_gas projects ($97.6B).

Canada posted a $1.8B merchandise trade surplus in March, its first since September 2025, reversing a $5.1B February deficit, as exports to the U.S. rose 8.3% and non-U.S. exports hit an all-time high (+9.1% month-over-month).107 Unemployment rose to 6.9% in April from 6.7% in March, with 18,000 jobs lost and youth unemployment at 14.3%.108 The week ahead brings the April CPI and housing-starts prints on May 17, the Q1 2026 national accounts in late May, and the next Bank of Canada decision on June 10.106

national.analysis:
Canada's real GDP contracted at an annualized rate of -0.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 against a consensus expectation of flat output, and full-year 2025 growth was 1.7%, the slowest pace since 2016 excluding the pandemic, according to Statistics Canada.112 Lower exports, particularly to the U.S. under steel, aluminum and motor-vehicle tariffs, were the main 2025 drag. StatCan reported that three in ten manufacturers cited a major negative tariff impact and one in five plan to delay investment.112

Industry GDP movements were mixed. Manufacturing output fell 3.1% year-over-year (NAICS 31-33) even as it rose 1.8% on the month; the database tracks 73 manufacturing projects ($68.8B).112 Mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21) rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.6% year-over-year, with 390 projects ($227.1B) tracked. Construction (NAICS 23) declined 0.5% month-over-month, while transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) rose 1.2% month-over-month and 4.5% year-over-year, aligning with 612 transport_logistics projects ($44.1B). Management of companies (NAICS 55) recorded a 22.3% year-over-year decline and utilities (NAICS 22) fell 4.0% year-over-year.

The Labour Force Survey recorded unemployment at 6.9% in April, up 0.2 percentage points from 6.7% in March, as the economy shed 18,000 positions.108 Youth unemployment reached 14.3% and the long-term unemployment share was 22.5%. The employment rate eased to 60.5% while participation held at 65.0%. Indeed Hiring Lab characterized the labour market as "stuck in neutral."81 SEPH wage growth ran at +3.9% year-over-year on a February reference, and The Hub reported 112,000 private-sector jobs lost year-to-date in 2026 alongside public-sector hiring cuts.22

Canada posted a $1.8B merchandise trade surplus in March, its first since September 2025, reversing a $5.1B February deficit, a $6.9B swing.107 The surplus with the U.S. widened to $7.1B as exports to the U.S. rose 8.3%, led by crude oil and passenger vehicles, while non-U.S. exports hit an all-time high (+9.1% month-over-month) on metal, mineral and energy products. The database tracks 390 mining projects ($227.1B) and 59 oil_gas projects ($97.6B).

CMHC's March housing-starts monthly SAAR fell 6% to 235,852 units from 250,961 in February, with the six-month trend easing to 248,378.62 Actual starts in centres of 10,000 or more population were 16,398 units, +10% year-over-year, with Montreal +26%, Toronto +23% and Vancouver +21% on multi-unit construction. Headline CPI rose 2.4% year-over-year in March, up from 1.8% in February, on a record 21.2% month-over-month gasoline increase; core CPI median ran at 2.3%, shelter +1.5% and food 5.3%.106 The database tracks 211 residential projects ($32.2B) and 1,663 infrastructure projects ($210.3B) carrying rate-sensitive financing while the Bank of Canada holds at 2.25%.

Ontario's unemployment rate stood at 7.5% in April 20261, above the national 6.9%. Ontario Budget 2026 projects the provincial rate easing from 7.7% in 2025 to 7.4% in 20262. The province added 80,900 net jobs in 2025; Budget 2026 anticipates softer 2026 job growth tied to slower population growth from federal immigration changes2.

Ontario CPI was +2.9% year-over-year, the highest among the four largest provinces, while provincial GDP growth registered +1.2%1. Provincial economic accounts (most recent available, Q3 2025) recorded exports of $638,705M (+4.3%) and goods GDP of $177,899M (-1.5%).

Honda indefinitely suspended its $15B Ontario EV and battery investment at Alliston3; the corresponding records are tagged Cancelled and excluded from the active pipeline, so the suspended amount is not counted toward active provincial capital value. The project database tracks 728 Ontario projects with roughly $360B in stated value, led by infrastructure (31 valued projects, ~$123B) including the $27.4B Ontario Line and $26.1B GO Expansion. Ontario Budget 2026 sets a $210B ten-year capital plan linked to 412 tracked projects2. Agnico Eagle's Northeastern Ontario Mining Expansion ($14B) advanced from Proposed to Approved4.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.analysis:
Quebec employment fell 43,300 in April 2026 (-0.9%)1, with cumulative 2026 losses near 87,000 jobs2. About half the losses concentrated in construction and manufacturing and roughly one quarter in financial services; the unemployment rate rose to 6.2%1.

Quebec CPI was -0.4% year-over-year, the lowest among provinces, while provincial GDP growth registered +1.3%. Provincial accounts (most recent available, Q3 2025) recorded real GDP of $486,872.74M (-0.1%) and exports of $208,930M (+0.2%)3.

The construction and manufacturing job losses align with a construction-intensive pipeline. The project database tracks 520 Quebec projects with roughly $78.4B in stated value: power and energy leads with 29 valued projects (~$35.4B), followed by mining (23 projects, ~$19.9B) and infrastructure (17 projects, ~$18.1B) including the Montreal Metro Blue Line extension, TramCite and REM branches. Quebec Budget 2026-27 carries a $167B infrastructure plan linked to 289 tracked projects3. Telesat Lightspeed has invested $1.8B with 600 Quebec jobs4.
provinces.sectorHighlights: Power and energy leads Quebec's tracked pipeline with 29 valued projects (~$35.4B), including the $9.0B Parc eolien zone Chamouchouane Hydro-Quebec wind farm. Mining follows with 23 projects (~$19.9B), and infrastructure adds 17 projects (~$18.1B) covering the $4.9B Blue Line metro extension and the $3.8B Quebec City TramCite. Construction and manufacturing absorbed roughly half the 2026 job losses.
provinces.labourDeepDive: Quebec employment fell 43,300 in April 2026 (-0.9%); cumulative 2026 losses are near 87,000, about half in construction and manufacturing and roughly one quarter in financial services. The unemployment rate rose to 6.2%. Participation rate was 64.4% and the employment rate 60.4%. Weekly earnings were $1,280.65 in February 2026.

The negative CPI print accompanies the largest single-month 2026 employment decline among large provinces (-43,300 in April), framing household conditions; Quebec manufacturing sales were $228,889M in March 2026.
provinces.marketContext: Quebec's tracked pipeline spans 520 projects with ~$78.4B in stated value. Largest components are power/energy (29 valued projects, ~$35.4B), mining (23 projects, ~$19.9B), and infrastructure (17 projects, ~$18.1B). Hydro-Quebec wind capacity and lithium mining tie the pipeline to power demand and critical-mineral pricing; CAD/USD moves flow through to the manufacturing base that absorbed part of the 2026 job losses.

ATB raised Alberta's 2026 real GDP forecast to 2.7% from 2.1% and nominal GDP to +6%, citing higher oil prices and a 2026 WTI forecast near US$75/bbl1; indicators carry provincial GDP growth at +2.7%. Alberta unemployment was 7.0% in April 2026, in line with the national rate, with roughly 85,000 jobs added over the prior year3.

One report states the fiscal position could move from a ~$9.4B deficit to a ~$6B surplus if elevated oil prices are sustained2. Alberta CPI was +1.3% year-over-year. The Canada-Alberta Co-operation Agreement on environmental and impact assessment, signed April 2, 2026, caps assessment timelines at two years4; the Flipi Gas-Fired Generation Project (460 MW, TransAlta) was Approved via IAAC early decision after a 64-day review.

The project database tracks 733 Alberta projects with roughly $346.9B in stated value: power and energy leads with 74 valued projects (~$137.3B), followed by manufacturing (17 projects, ~$65.8B) and oil and gas (16 projects, ~$44.4B). The $50B Olds AI Data Centre Hub is the largest single first-tracked record. WTI and WCS price moves flow through to the Pathways Alliance carbon capture hub ($16.5B) and Dow's net-zero facility ($11.5B).

Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP contracted 1.3% month-over-month while holding +3.5% year-over-year115. Lead export commodities remained elevated: wheat priced $655, up 22.9% Y/Y and 7.8% W/W, while Western SPF lumber held $584.50/mfbm, up 5.2% Y/Y72. The project database tracks 14 discrete projects ($4.74B) — roughly 2 agriculture and 12 forestry — a research-led rather than project-led pipeline24. The 12 forestry projects ($4.73B) sit against U.S. Section 232 plus AD/CVD measures that raise Canadian producer costs an estimated 25-30%; Western Forest Products extended its Chemainus, B.C. sawmill closure through end of 2026103.

Sector capital flows largely through policy channels. Farm Credit Canada convened a coalition of 20+ investment organizations prepared to deploy up to $5 billion by 2030, totalling $7 billion with FCC's May 2025 commitment71. The five-year $3.5-billion Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership continues, with $75 million added over five years to AgriMarketing market-diversification streams36. If U.S. trade measures persist, additional sawmill closures and rural employment contraction would extend the forestry sub-sector divergence from the +3.5% Y/Y aggregate.

goodsIndustries.analysis:

Electra Battery Materials received a $20 million federal Strategic Response Fund investment toward a $99.4 million cobalt-sulfate refinery expansion in Temiskaming Shores, Ontario, part of the Critical Minerals Strategy battery build-out; Northvolt QC funding ended in September 202542. February's month-over-month momentum reverses the negative Y/Y trend, with January 2026 production at -4.20% Y/Y. If the PMI expansion holds, the Y/Y comparison would narrow through Q2 2026; if U.S. tariff uncertainty intensifies, the EV/battery project set would face delivery risk, as the Honda suspension already illustrates.

industry_executive_summary:
February industry GDP was mixed across the 20 NAICS sectors. Among goods producers, manufacturing rose 1.8% month-over-month, its largest gain since January 2023, while remaining -3.1% year-over-year; the database tracks 73 manufacturing projects ($68.8B), excluding the suspended Honda Ontario $15B EV plant recorded as Cancelled. Mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.6% year-over-year, while agriculture fell 1.3%, construction 0.5%, and utilities held flat at -4.0% year-over-year.

Among services, transportation and warehousing rose 1.2% month-over-month (+4.5% year-over-year) and finance and insurance rose 0.3% (+2.9% year-over-year), while management of companies posted the largest decline at -2.6% month-over-month and -22.3% year-over-year. Real estate and health care were both flat on the month, up 1.4% and 2.1% year-over-year respectively.

financialMarkets.fx_commentary: The Canadian dollar eased to 0.7276 against the U.S. dollar, down 0.6% on the week and up 1.6% year-over-year, with USD/CAD at 1.3743 — driven by the wide Bank of Canada–Federal Reserve policy gap, which held the loonie soft even as WTI crude traded near US$100/bbl64. The Bank of Canada's 2.25% policy rate sits roughly 138 basis points below the Federal Reserve's 3.50%-3.75% target midpoint after both central banks held in late April, a differential that continued to favour U.S.-dollar carry over crude-linked Canadian-dollar support2663. EUR/USD slipped 0.8% on the week to 1.1640, though it remained 3.6% above its year-ago level, as Bloomberg-surveyed economists positioned for two ECB quarter-point hikes in 2026 against the energy-driven inflation backdrop32. USD/JPY rose 1.1% to 158.49 and stands 9.3% above a year ago, while USD/CNY was little changed at 6.81. The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine ties the softer loonie to the 73 manufacturing projects valued at $68.8B exposed to cross-border trade. If the loonie holds near its current soft level against the greenback through the CUSMA review window, those 73 trade-exposed manufacturing projects would face the input-cost and tariff conditions documented in the March merchandise trade data. CAD/USD at 0.7276 frames that exposure107.

commodity_commentary: Commodity markets were led higher this week by energy, where WTI crude rose 4.97% to US$100.16/bbl and Brent gained 7.21% to US$108.59/bbl, both driven by Strait of Hormuz supply disruption flagged in the May IEA Oil Market Report.82 Natural gas added 5.88% to US$2.92/MMBtu while remaining 14.82% below a year ago. Precious metals diverged from energy: gold fell 3.33% to US$4,563.20/oz and silver eased 2.00% to US$78.79/oz, though gold held a 39.1% year-over-year gain after record Q1 2026 global demand reported by the World Gold Council83. Base metals firmed, with copper up 1.47% to US$6.34/lb on resilient Chinese demand after Q1 2026 GDP printed 5.0%60. Agriculture moved with wheat up 7.82% to 655.00c/bu and potash up 4.34% on the Nutrien proxy; lumber added 1.39% to US$584.50/mfbm. The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine ties the energy move to 59 oil and gas projects ($97.6B) and the metals strength to the resource pipeline within the database's 7,480 tracked projects valued at $1,472.2B51. Western Canadian Select, uranium, nickel and canola carried no priced series in the data this week and are marked unavailable.
consumer_pulse:
Cost-of-living attention concentrated on gasoline. The national average pump price rose to $1.92/L on May 12 from $1.87/L on May 5, about +3% in a week, with Newfoundland and Labrador highest at $2.09/L and Alberta lowest at $1.79/L.73 StatCan's March gasoline component rose a record 21.2% month-over-month and 5.9% year-over-year.106 Reddit and Google Trends signals tracked "gas prices" (sentiment -0.7, frequency 19), "oil shock / Middle East war" (-0.6), "inflation" (-0.5) and "cost of living" (-0.6) as the dominant themes.

Wages have outpaced prices for more than three years, with SEPH wage growth at +3.9% year-over-year, partially offsetting cost pressure.22 Rental affordability shifted: the national rent-to-income ratio fell to 29%, below the 30% threshold for the first time in more than six years, and average rent declined 5.3% year-over-year to $2,008.95 The lowest five-year fixed mortgage rate was about 4.04%, edging up as energy-driven inflation lifts fixed rates; CIBC reported 70% of prospective buyers say conditions are too uncertain to judge timing.61 Labour-market unease registered in trending topics on "jobs lost" (frequency 14), "youth unemployment" and "layoffs" after April recorded 18,000 jobs lost, unemployment at 6.9%, youth unemployment at 14.3% and a long-term unemployment share of 22.5%.108 "U.S. tariffs" (frequency 15) and "economic uncertainty" (frequency 14) remained persistent threads.

marketCommentary:
North American equity indices advanced and crude extended its run in the week ending May 14 — the S&P/TSX Composite rose +1.2% to 34,26823, while the S&P 500 gained +2.2% to 7,501 and the Nasdaq added +3.2% to 26,635. WTI crude settled at US$100.16/bbl, up +5.0% on the week and +60.1% year over year, with Brent at US$108.59/bbl (+7.2%) following the Strait of Hormuz supply disruption6482. The Canadian dollar eased -0.6% to 0.7276 CAD/USD. The database tracks 7,480 active and proposed projects valued at $1,472.2 billion.

The project pipeline's exposure split between rate-sensitive financing and commodity pricing — the database contains 211 residential projects ($32.2 billion) and 1,663 infrastructure projects ($210.3 billion) that carry rate-sensitive financing against the Bank of Canada's 2.25% policy rate and a 6.09% prime rate26. The 10-year Government of Canada yield stood at 3.56%, up from 3.06% a year earlier, with the 2-10 spread at 60 basis points. The database also tracks 59 oil and gas projects ($97.6 billion) and 390 mining projects ($227.1 billion); if WTI holds above US$100, these energy projects price against a level +60.1% above the year-ago benchmark82.

yieldCurveCommentary: The Government of Canada curve held a normal, upward slope, with the 2Y at 2.96% and the 10Y at 3.56% for a 2s10s spread of about 60 basis points — steeper than the roughly 49 basis points recorded a year ago, reflecting global term-premium repricing as the synchronized G7 central-bank hold met an energy-driven inflation regime31. Prior-week tenor levels were unavailable, so moves are measured against year-ago levels. Against a year ago, the 2Y is up about 39 basis points from 2.57% and the 10Y up about 50 basis points from 3.06%, with the Long bond up roughly 61 basis points to 3.91% — the steepest year-over-year back-up on the curve. The Bank of Canada's fourth consecutive hold at 2.25% on April 29 anchored the front end while ECB tightening expectations and the BoE's second consecutive hold pushed the global long end higher2667. The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine links the rate path to 1,663 infrastructure projects ($210.3B) and 211 residential projects ($32.2B) carrying rate-sensitive financing exposure. If the yields tracked here hold near current levels rather than retreating, those rate-sensitive infrastructure and residential projects, totalling roughly two hundred forty billion dollars with commercial-adjacent exposure, would carry financing costs consistent with the held policy rate rather than the lower term yields seen a year earlier48.
